Question: Will inflation increase if Trump lowers the price of gas? Will people have more discretionary spending for the mall?
Answer: Even though it isn't easily visible to consumers, there is a downside to oil prices being too low as well as too high. American oil companies are not the year-after-year money-making machines that the press would have you believe, because their costs of recovery (drilling and refining) vary much less than the price at which they can sell their end products. When worldwide economic activity slowed during the COVID crisis in February and March 2020, Saudi Arabia led an OPEC movement to cut production to stabilize prices. But Russia wasn't willing to go along — they saw production cuts by others as an opportunity to increase their market share. Well, this pissed the Saudis off, and since Saudi Arabia can bring their oil to market at a much lower cost than pretty much every other country (for geological reasons), they decided to flood the market and drive the price low enough to make it unprofitable for Russia. Unfortunately, the U.S. companies got caught in this crossfire and they also saw their margins erode. In early April President Trump stepped in and helped negotiate an agreement to stop this production war and balance the needs of producers and consumers. (My independent professional research at that time showed that the optimal price for oil was one that would result in an average price for regular gasoline of $2.69.)
